Syntax Comparison Matrix (Measured)

This page compares the syntax capabilities of Rust and SLA item by item, and explains what the goal of a “Rust surface-compatible subset” actually means: which Rust spellings can be pasted in directly, which are silently absorbed, and which will never be accepted. After reading it you will be able to estimate how much a piece of Rust code needs to change to move to SLA.

NoteThe matrix on this page comes from docs/rust_vs_sla_final_cn.md §2.A (snapshot of 2026-06-15) and the surface compatibility assessment report from the same day. It is a point-in-time measured framing, not a permanent commitment; for the current maturity of each feature, see the “SLA Language Reference” chapter.

Target Positioning: A “Rust Surface-Compatible Subset”

SLA's goal has never been to “become Rust”, but rather:

Let a large amount of Rust code parse as-is in SLA, with the compiler silently absorbing Rust's redundant surface declarations (lifetime / pub / where) into SA's implicit behavior during lowering.

That way an LLM or a human can paste Rust-style code directly, and the SLA compiler plays the role of “translator + intelligent filter”, while preserving all of SA's safety constraints. By the 2026-06-15 assessment framing: Phase 1 about 70% surface compatibility (let mut x, &mut T, &mut self all need manual removal of mut); Phase 2 about 85% (after introducing &mut T/&mut self, let mut is still never introduced). Semantically the target is “the Rust safe single-threaded subset − Drop trait − full lifetimes − proc-macro”.

Silent Absorption: Parsed but Semantically Emptied

Rust syntaxSLA handlingReason
let mut x = ...Never acceptedSLA's let is already mutable by default, so mut is silently misleading instead
&mut TNot introduced in Phase 1; introduced in Phase 2 (before the sa3d ECS launch)Currently &T covers read and write
fn foo(&mut self)Not recognized in Phase 1 (mut must be removed manually); introduced in Phase 2 as a separate exclusive-borrow contractSame as above
'a / 'staticParsed but not carried into semanticsSA does not build a cross-function borrow graph
pub / pub(crate)Parsed and discardedSA defaults to everything being linker-visible
unsafe { ... } / unsafe fnParsed and discarded; when raw pointers are involved, the code must be wrapped in @ffi_wrapperSLA replaces block-level unsafe with function-level isolation
where T: Bound / <T: Bound>Loud error (ruled 2026-10-29): SLA does not support generic bounds — the historical implementation parsed and silently discarded bounds (an empty shell: the parser only consumed the bound name without saving it, and the AST / checker / monomorphization had no representation of bounds, so even a bound pointing at a nonexistent trait passed checking); it has now been ruled that writing a bound is a compile error (see the addendum in section 7 of document 15)Trait method dispatch relies on an explicit impl registry + monomorphization and has nothing to do with whether a bound was written; no bound solving is introduced
#[derive(...)] / #[inline]Mapped to the existing @derive(...) / inlineSame semantics, different skin

Looks Like Rust, Semantically Different

Surface spellingActual semanticsPromise to developers
let mut xNever acceptedSLA and Rust have reversed default mutability
&TCurrently covers both read and write usesAfter lowering it is always SA &; the Referee physical layer is unchanged
Drop traitNot supportedStill implicitly injected by the compiler as !; users cannot write impl Drop
'a annotationsParsed onlyCross-function borrowing safety is borne by the frontend responsibility model, with no checking
unsafe blocksDegrade to a “declaration of intent”Real pointer descent is allowed only at the @ffi_wrapper function level; raw-pointer operations inside a block require the enclosing function to be marked @ffi_wrapper, otherwise an error
panic!("...")panic(code) numeric codeThe string variant goes through sa_std's panic_msg
Send/SyncParsed onlyActually backed by the Referee's affine mask + cross-core validation; no trait solving is exposed

Spellings Explicitly Refused

  • let mut x (permanently refused; conflicts with SLA's current let = mutable)
  • The Drop trait; implicit GC / unwind / panic catch
  • Full NLL / Polonius-style lifetime inference
  • Arbitrarily complex expansion of proc-macro and macro_rules! (SLA's hygienic macros are kept; println! and the like go through hard-coded paths)
  • &mut existing as a separate type in lowered SA — Phase 2 will introduce &mut T at the source level, but after lowering it is still SA &

Exact Parsing Rules for ^ and !

^ does not conflict with Rust's XOR, because the two appear in different parser positions:

prefix  '^' expr          → Move（Sla 既有）
expr '^' expr             → XOR（Rust 风）
'^' 出现在 type 位置       → 非法

Discrimination method: when ^ appears, look at whether there is an expression ending on the left that can serve as an operand (identifier/literal/)/]). If yes → infix XOR; if no → prefix Move.

// 同一行里两种含义可以共存
let moved = ^payload;              // 前缀：move
let flags = a ^ b;                 // 中缀：XOR

There are three positions for !:

prefix '!' expr           → 逻辑非（唯一接受语义）
ident '!' (...)           → 短期不引入（与 SA 的 ! 释放原语视觉冲突）
单独 '!' 后跟寄存器        → SA 释放原语，仅生成的 .sa 与 @debug 模式可见
NoteThis is “not introduced in the short term” rather than “never introduced”. It will be re-evaluated once SA's ! has completely disappeared from the .sla user surface. Until then, the parser does a fault-tolerant downgrade for a ! immediately adjacent to an identifier: it strips it as syntactic noise and rewrites println!("x") to println("x") and continues parsing.

Key Points of This Page

  • Core features such as structs/enums/closures/generics/?/async have similar shapes on both sides; what is truly reversed is the mutability default.
  • Surface compatibility is “Rust style in, SA semantics out”: lifetime/pub/where are silently absorbed, and let mut is permanently refused.
  • Prefix move ^ and infix XOR do not conflict; they are split by parser context.
  • For mutability details see the Ownership and Borrowing: Referee vs the Borrow Checker page; for @overload/@derive details see the Macros and Metaprogramming Compared page.
